vignette:
The Weight of the Corridor

Kofi is a 77-year-old Ghanaian man who has spent the better part of five decades shaping young minds. He walks the hallways of his primary school with a deliberate, measured pace - the kind that comes from decades of authority, of knowing that children watch the way a principal carries himself. He has always believed that a school is a sanctuary. That belief was shattered fourteen months ago.

It happened on a Thursday evening, after the last teachers had gone home. Kofi was locking the administrative block when two men entered through the side gate. What began as what he assumed was a robbery turned into something far more brutal. He was beaten with a metal pipe - his ribs fractured, his left forearm broken, his face bloodied against the concrete floor. He remembers the sound of his own voice begging, and he remembers the shame of that more than almost anything else. He lay on the floor of his own school for nearly two hours before the night watchman found him.

His body healed, more or less. His wife, Abena, nursed him through the physical recovery with quiet devotion. But Kofi has not been the same man since that Thursday evening, and both of them know it.

He returned to work after six weeks because he did not know what else to do with himself. The school is his identity - he has been its principal for nineteen years. But now the administrative block feels wrong to him. He re-routes his morning walk to avoid the exact corridor where it happened, adding several unnecessary minutes to his day. His deputy has noticed. Kofi has offered no explanation.

At night, he does not sleep so much as he endures the hours. He lies rigid beside Abena, listening to sounds in the compound - a gate swinging, a dog, footsteps on gravel - and his heart begins to pound before his mind has even fully registered what he heard. He has woken her three times in recent weeks, convinced that someone was inside the house. Each time, there was no one. He does not apologize for waking her. He cannot explain the certainty he feels in those moments, the absolute animal conviction that something terrible is about to happen again.

The flashbacks come most often in the late afternoon, when the school empties. He will be sitting at his desk reviewing attendance records or signing letters, and without warning he is back on that floor - the cold concrete against his cheek, the sound of the pipe, the smell of his own blood. He returns to the present disoriented and sweating, sometimes to find that his hands have been gripping the edge of the desk hard enough to whiten his knuckles.

He has become short with his staff in ways that embarrass him afterward. A teacher who came to him flustered and speaking too quickly last month found herself facing a fury she did not understand. Kofi understood it even less. He has always prided himself on his composure, on being the calm center of a busy institution. That composure feels like a performance now, and an exhausting one.

He has stopped attending the men's fellowship at his church, where he has worshipped for forty years. He tells Abena it is because he is tired. The truth is that he cannot sit in a room where he does not have a clear view of the door.

Kofi does not speak about what happened - not to Abena, not to his pastor, not to the colleagues who were told only that he had been the victim of a break-in. In his culture, in his generation, and in the particular dignity of his position, there is no language for what he carries. He was a man who protected children. He could not protect himself. He sits with that knowledge every day, behind a desk in a school he built, in a corridor he can no longer walk through.
